purpose: Synthetic behavioral cases for argument review; this is an answer-key case pack, not a validator report or evidence of an executed review.

Resolve only explicit fixture references. Extract the named Proposal Text section through its Aim 3 paragraph and stop before the closing commentary paragraph beginning These aims do not overlap. Supply review_context only after recording the source-only findings, except SC13: its explicitly pre-exposed context must accompany that case and its reviewer must report the isolation limitation.
A mixed package is a list of separately identified source documents. Review routing must be decided per document function.
Do not open an unavailable source or figure or discover replacements. These examples contain no real application, external citations, measured results, or private scientific context.
Compare the actual findings with expected only after the reviewer has returned its review. An expected result is not an observed smoke-test result.

Program overview, paragraph 1: This ambitious and timely program will transform our understanding of soft actuators. Its primary goal is to characterize and compensate for response-time variation across actuator surfaces and fabrication routes. Our coordinated strategy combines precise measurements, rigorous comparison, and elegant control.

Aim 1, paragraph 1: We will map the relationship between interface roughness and actuator response time using a controlled roughness series. This innovative work will produce a high-resolution response-time map.

Aim 2, paragraph 1: We will compare three fabrication routes while holding the actuator geometry fixed. This exciting comparison will reveal route-specific response-time differences.

Aim 3, paragraph 1: We will build a controller that compensates for response-time differences measured in standardized trials. This important development will deliver a benchmarked controller.

Integration, paragraph 1: The map, fabrication comparison, and controller address the same response-time variation from complementary measurement, manufacturing, and control perspectives.

previous_findings.finding: No reason is given why uncertainty about response-time variation matters.
previous_findings.resolution_condition: The current text must identify the important uncertainty or limitation that remains without this work and explain how the program's knowledge gain addresses it.

previous_findings.finding: Aim-level outputs have no explanation of why each matters.
previous_findings.resolution_condition: Each of Aims 1, 2, and 3 must connect its expected knowledge gain to a stated scientific or enabling limitation.

Program, paragraph 1: Our shared robotic test platform enables three equally central goals: minimizing warehouse delivery time, explaining how abrasive contact alters ceramic wear, and developing a mathematical taxonomy of collective motion. Each direction will occupy one third of the program.

Project A, paragraph 1: Congestion makes delivery schedules unreliable. We do not know when local routing rules create network-wide queues. Controlled robot traffic will identify those conditions, enabling scheduling rules that avoid queue formation and advancing the delivery-time goal.

Project B, paragraph 1: Wear models do not distinguish the contribution of repeated contact from that of surface geometry. Robotic abrasion trials will isolate these contributions, improving explanations of material degradation and advancing the ceramic-wear goal.

Project C, paragraph 1: Similar group trajectories can arise from different local interaction rules. We will classify which observable trajectory features distinguish those rules, clarifying the relation between local interaction and collective order and advancing the taxonomy goal.

Shared resources, paragraph 1: All projects use the same robots, tracking cameras, and analysis workstation.

required_findings: A common tool platform does not establish a single shared scientific objective.
The three equally central objectives lack a stated primary goal or priority relation.
Request an author priority decision and compare a minimum explanatory repair with a materially different prioritization option, retaining Candidate 0 and tradeoffs.
forbidden_findings: Invent that delivery optimization, ceramic wear, or collective motion is the author's real primary goal.
Order deletion of scientifically valuable directions solely because their topics differ.

source.text:
Program, paragraph 1: Similar elastic networks can relax at different rates, limiting a general explanation of how local structure produces macroscopic dynamics. The unresolved gap is whether connectivity and boundary constraints explain distinct parts of that variation or merely substitute for one another in effective models. The primary goal is to identify which features determine relaxation laws and the conditions under which those laws generalize. Closing this gap matters for fundamental statistical mechanics: without it, models with different microscopic explanations can remain indistinguishable at the bulk level, and their claimed generality cannot be assessed.

Aim 1, paragraph 1: We will establish how connectivity changes relaxation scaling at fixed boundary conditions. This isolates the connectivity contribution that current effective descriptions cannot distinguish. The expected knowledge gain is a map of which connectivity properties preserve a scaling law and which change it. That distinction matters because it separates a general law from a fit to one network family. Aim 1 contributes the local-structure component of the program's explanation.

Aim 2, paragraph 1: We will establish how boundary constraints change relaxation scaling at fixed connectivity. This isolates boundary effects that could otherwise be mistaken for a microscopic law. The expected knowledge gain is a set of conditions under which bulk behavior is insensitive or sensitive to the boundary. These conditions matter because they define when a finite-network observation supports a general theoretical claim. Aim 2 contributes the boundary-condition component of the same explanation.

Integration, paragraph 1: Both Aims have equal priority and can proceed independently using predefined network ensembles. Neither requires the other's success. Their complementary comparisons jointly distinguish connectivity-driven and boundary-driven explanations of the same relaxation laws; integration consists of comparing their domains of validity within a common theoretical description.

Future horizon, paragraph 1: A later extension could ask whether driven networks obey analogous principles. That question is outside the current program's deliverables and resource allocation; it is a future horizon after the present theory is assessed, not a third current Aim. No immediate application or clinical outcome is claimed.

required_findings: The two independent Aims explicitly make complementary contributions to one goal.
Fundamental-science significance is explicit and sufficient for this argument scope.
The future horizon is not an immediate third deliverable.
READY is limited to the argument scope and does not predict a hiring result.
forbidden_findings: Require serial dependency, removal of one Aim, immediate clinical relevance, or an additional significance heading.
Manufacture a substantive defect solely to avoid a positive verdict.

Program, paragraph 1: Sensor offsets change during extended use. The unresolved question is how offset depends on temperature history and housing stiffness. The primary goal is to characterize these two sources of offset variation.

Aim 1, paragraph 1: We will cycle temperature to isolate the effect of temperature history and record the resulting sensor traces.

Aim 2, paragraph 1: We will compare housing stiffnesses to isolate their effect on offset, learning how the offset-stiffness relationship changes at fixed temperature.

Integration, paragraph 1: The two Aims independently characterize temperature and housing contributions to the same offset variation. Both have equal priority.

source.text:
Program, paragraph 1: Actuator response-time variation can reflect interface physics, fabrication differences, or limitations of a control model. These explanations are not yet separated in a common account of response timing. Our primary goal is to determine when response timing can be predicted and compensated across surface and fabrication variation. This matters because otherwise a timing model that fits one actuator may be mistaken for a general explanation, and the conditions limiting its transfer remain unknown.

Aim 1, paragraph 1: We will vary interface roughness at fixed geometry and fabrication route to isolate the surface contribution. The expected gain is the relationship between roughness and response timing, including where that relationship changes. This matters because it distinguishes surface-dependent timing from a route-dependent artifact. Aim 1 supplies the surface component of the program's account of predictable timing.

Aim 2, paragraph 1: We will compare fabrication routes at matched geometry and roughness to isolate fabrication-dependent variation. The expected gain is knowledge of which timing relationships persist across routes. This matters because persistence or failure across routes defines the scope of a general timing explanation. Aim 2 supplies the transfer conditions for the program's predictive account.

Aim 3, paragraph 1: We will test a compensating controller across prespecified timing variations to distinguish variation representable by a shared model from variation that needs route-specific parameters. The expected gain is the boundary between transferable and route-specific compensation. This matters because successful compensation on one device alone cannot establish that its model captures variation across devices. Aim 3 contributes a functional test of the program's claim about predictable and compensable timing.

Integration, paragraph 1: These equally prioritized Aims examine surface effects, fabrication transfer, and model sufficiency within one objective. Standardized actuator sets let each Aim produce an interpretable result independently; together their comparisons delimit where a shared timing model applies.

Each of Aims 1, 2, and 3 must connect its expected knowledge gain to a stated scientific or enabling limitation.

source.text:
Program, paragraph 1: A measured timing difference can arise from the clock or from the measurement setup, limiting interpretation of small timing variations. The unresolved gap is how to separate these contributions when the setup changes. Our primary goal is to identify timing differences that persist across independent measurement arrangements. This matters because, without that distinction, setup artifacts and properties of the clock remain competing explanations of the same observation.

Project, paragraph 1: We will compare the same clock under two independently configured readout arrangements. Varying the arrangement while preserving the clock isolates the setup contribution. The expected knowledge gain is which timing differences are invariant to the readout and which depend on it. That distinction matters because invariance constrains whether a timing claim can be attributed to the clock. This single project directly supplies the invariant-versus-setup-dependent distinction needed by the primary goal.

Scope, paragraph 1: Figure 1 would illustrate the two arrangements; the argument and project definition are fully stated above and make no evidential claim about an unseen result.

documents.text: Curriculum vitae: Research role in measurement engineering. Experience in instrument calibration, project coordination, and student supervision. Skills: data analysis and technical writing.
Resume: Measurement engineer with experience maintaining calibration schedules, documenting instrument checks, and coordinating equipment use.

Dear Search Committee, I am applying for the advertised research position. My training in measurement engineering and experience supervising projects fit the described role. Please find my research statement and curriculum vitae enclosed.

Dear Search Committee, I recommend the candidate based on direct supervision of a measurement engineering project. The candidate documented assumptions clearly, coordinated shared equipment, and responded constructively to review.

My interest in engineering grew through repairing classroom instruments. I value collaborative learning and clear explanations, and I hope to develop as a mentor while contributing to an inclusive research environment.

Program, paragraph 1: Calibration results can vary with the sequence of applied loads, obstructing a consistent interpretation of sensor response. The knowledge gap is whether this history dependence reflects reversible lag or persistent change. My primary goal is to distinguish those two explanations. The distinction matters because they imply different conditions under which a calibration relation can be generalized beyond one load sequence.

Research direction, paragraph 1: I will compare responses to reordered load sequences with defined recovery intervals. This comparison separates order effects from changes that persist after recovery. The expected knowledge gain is the boundary between reversible and persistent history effects; that boundary matters because it determines when a history-independent calibration claim is justified. This single direction directly addresses the primary goal by discriminating the two explanations.
